But it has a steep learning curve, and … Read the full story at The Verge. ]]> Andrew Liszewski https://www.theverge.com/?p=993521 2026-09-29T11:54:53-04:00 2026-10-02T09:00:00-04:00 Although I count the original Game Boy as one of my first tech obsessions, I still consider Nintendo’s Game Boy Advance to be my favorite console of all time thanks to its more comfortable horizontal design (for my big hands) and its expansive catalog of excellent 32-bit and 16-bit games. Ayaneo isn’t the first company to attempt to modernize the GBA, but its Konkr Pocket Advance does it best. The handheld strikes a near perfect balance between authentically re-creating the GBA’s design while updating its hardware with new controls, a much better screen, and the flexibility of Android at a price that feels like a bargain. As much as I still adore the GBA, I’ve eagerly embraced upgrades to the aging console over the years. First it was the clamshell GBA SP that finally delivered a frontlit screen I could actually see without a lamp over my shoulder, and later it was aftermarket upgrades like a backlit LCD display and a rechargeable battery that vastly improved Nintendo’s original hardware. Two years ago, I eagerly purchased Anbernic’s GBA-inspired RG34XX , but all of those have now been replaced by the Konkr Pocket Advance. It’s my first handheld from Ayaneo, and I’ve been pleasantly surprised to find the hardware feels on par with Nintendo’s. The Pocket Advance is an all-plastic affair but with a satisfying heft thanks to extra internal hardware including a cooling fan for its MediaTek Helio G90T processor and a 4,000mAh battery. I opted for the cheaper $109 version with 3GB of RAM and 32GB of storage, which is expandable with a microSD card, but for $129, you can get 4GB of RAM with 64GB of storage built-in. It’s not an exact copy of the GBA, but the Pocket Advance’s dimensions are close enough to fit all the cases I’ve somehow preserved for the past 25 years. Where Ayaneo’s remake really diverges from the original is with eight additional buttons including X and Y action buttons plus four extra shoulder buttons on the top edge. I’m a big fan of the larger D-pad Ayaneo has included, but some retro gaming purists may not be fans of how soft and squishy the Pocket Advance’s buttons all feel. I’ve had to learn to mash the action buttons just a little harder to ensure presses are always registered, but I don’t necessarily think the button feel is a downside because they’re also satisfyingly quiet. The Pocket Advance’s 3.5-inch LCD touchscreen with a glass cover is an excellent upgrade, but it does cater to GBA games with a 3:2 aspect ratio and a 960×640 resolution allowing them to be perfectly scaled at 4x. (The GBA had a 240×160 screen resolution.) Unless you’re a monster who can tolerate playing games that have been stretched vertically or horizontally to fill a screen, emulating games from other systems will result in letterboxing or pillarboxing on the sides, and potentially some visual artifacts from scaling when the math isn’t perfect. Most similarly sized and similarly priced handhelds run some variation of Linux. There’s a thriving community of developers creating and porting a large assortment of emulators, games, and apps to Linux, but installing, configuring, customizing and updating software is not always a user-friendly process, especially for novices who may only be familiar with using plug-and-play game carts.
